passages.title: Sporting and Performing Arts Opportunities for Pupils in State Schools
passages.speaker: Baroness Smith of Malvern (Lab)
passages.body: The right reverend Prelate is right that the HAF programme has provided both food and activities for very many children and young people. While we have provided 21 million days to children and young people in England, which have been delivered across 153 local authorities, notwithstanding the £600 million that has been committed to it, we need to look carefully at how we get that to as many children as possible. I cannot commit to changing the entitlement rules but I will take back the points that the right reverend Prelate has made on that programme.

passages.speaker: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (Vicky Foxcroft)
passages.body: also builds on the wider work this Government are doing to ensure more children and young people have access to high-quality enriching activities. This includes the £22.5 million enrichment expansion programme which is supporting 400 secondary schools to improve their enrichment offer, the £600 million—over the next three financial years—holiday and activities food programme which provides free holiday clubs and enriching activities during school holidays to children from low-income households, as well as the enrichment framework to support schools and colleges across England to strengthen their enrichment offer. These announcements form part of the Government’s wider

passages.title: Sporting and Performing Arts Opportunities for Pupils in State Schools
passages.speaker: The Lord Bishop of Leicester
passages.body: My Lords, the holiday activities and food programme is a shining example of the approach described by the noble Lord, Lord Addington. It offers a proven way of linking up children from disadvantaged backgrounds with a wide range of enriching activities during the school holidays. However, the current eligibility criteria result in more than 500,000 children, mostly from poorer working families, being unable to access the programme. Will the Minister commit to rectifying this by aligning the programme’s eligibility criteria with those that are attached to term-time free school meals?

passages.speaker: Baroness Sater (Con)
passages.body: My Lords, if we want more children to have access to sport and physical activity, we need to make better use of existing facilities. The Opening School Facilities programme helped open nearly 1,900 schools to their local communities but ended in March 2025. Given the demand from organisations which are keen to deliver activities, I ask the Minister to reconsider renewing the highly successful programme.

passages.title: Houses in Multiple Occupation
passages.speaker: The Minister for Housing and Planning (Matthew Pennycook)
passages.body: The new national planning policy framework, published on 17 August, includes a more flexible and proportionate policy design to provide greater clarity on the circumstances in which article 4 directions may be appropriate, including where there is an overconcentration of small HMOs. We want to ensure that councils can act properly to regulate HMOs where it is necessary to protect the amenity or wellbeing of an area, and we will continue to keep the powers to regulate HMOs under review.

passages.title: Houses in Multiple Occupation
passages.speaker: Matthew Pennycook
passages.body: I will congratulate the hon. Member’s local authority. As I say, it is through up-to-date local plans and strong policies on HMOs that local authorities can ensure that they are properly regulated. After all, development plans are the basis on which decision makers, irrespective of whether they are officers or committees, will make their decisions. There is good practice out there in the country—including in my own local authority area, as I have said—and I encourage any local planning authority with concerns to familiarise itself with that good practice.

passages.title: Homes and Planning Bill
passages.speaker: The Minister for Housing and Planning (Matthew Pennycook)
passages.body: To clarify for the hon. Gentleman, where an adopted up-to-date local plan was in place at the point we introduced the new national planning policy framework, its housing need requirement remained as per that adopted plan. Transitional arrangements were put in place. Yes, as the system progresses, local authorities will have to plan on the basis of the new standard method, but it is not the case to say that when we changed the NPPF in December 2024, immediately across the country those new targets kicked in everywhere.

passages.title: Impact of Defence Spending
passages.speaker: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Wales (Anna McMorrin)
passages.body: This Government are delivering the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the cold war by investing £298 billion over the next four years to strengthen our national security and keep us safe. Wales is well placed to benefit from this investment, with 20,000 defence jobs already in Wales. Every pound that we invest in defence should be judged by what it does. We want to ensure that all investment brings jobs and skills, and strengthens our national security.

passages.title: Impact of Defence Spending
passages.speaker: Charlie Dewhirst (Bridlington and The Wolds) (Con)
passages.body: The Welsh defence industry supports 20,000 jobs and is absolutely vital to the national security of the United Kingdom, yet defence firms face growing uncertainty over the UK Government’s failure to set out a detailed plan to meet the 3% of GDP target on defence spending and Plaid Cymru’s proposed defence ethical investment framework in Wales, which are both creating serious concern for businesses looking to invest, expand and protect jobs. Therefore, what discussions has the Minister had with defence companies about these concerns, and what is she doing to give the industry the certainty it

The Global Campaign on Military Spending says that it does not, finding that military spending, in fact, “has one of the lowest ‘employment multipliers’ of all economic categories. It ranks 70th in terms of the employment it generates, out of 100.” As such, my belief is that military spending will not bring the jobs that the industry claims it will. passages.speaker: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Wales (Anna McMorrin)
passages.body: I have regular discussions with the Welsh Government on defence and many other matters. We are fully funding the £15 billion defence investment plan, strengthening our armed forces, investing in cutting-edge technology and creating nearly 60,000 additional industry jobs across the UK. Continued uncertainty around the Welsh Government’s approach to defence, and delays to important projects such as DARC—Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability—risk deterring investment and jobs from Wales, as well as risking our national security.

passages.body: My Lords, the concerning levels of water in storage—17% beneath seasonal norms, as the Minister mentioned—reflects not just a dry year but systematic underinvestment by the water industry against long-standing forecasts for demand growth and climate change. What assessment have the Government made of the speed, cost and volume of improvement that is possible from nature-based solutions and on-farm reservoirs, versus the expense, controversy and long timelines of new reservoirs? I declare my interest as a farmer and landowner.

passages.title: Automobile Industry: ZEV Mandate
passages.speaker: Baroness in Waiting/Government Whip (Baroness Dacres of Lewisham) (Lab)
passages.body: The automotive sector’s future is zero emissions. The Government are investing more than £7.5 billion to drive investments and safeguard jobs for the future. Tata is investing £4 billion in the UK gigafactory, with further investments from Stellantis, Nissan, Bentley, McLaren and others. We are taking a balanced approach to the transition. We have just closed a consultation reviewing the ZEV mandate. We are working with the devolved Governments to publish the outcome as soon as possible.

passages.body: I was slightly surprised to hear the Opposition spokesperson’s comments in light of the investment that Tata Agratas is making in his constituency, which is creating hundreds of jobs at an electrification plant. Maybe he is just following the Opposition party lines, but I am sure Tata will be very disappointed to hear what he has said. I was deeply disappointed by the outcome of COP. passages.title: Automobile Industry: ZEV Mandate
passages.speaker: Baroness Dacres of Lewisham (Lab)
passages.body: I would like to reassure the noble Baroness that the work we are doing to make sure that we have direction, and are clear, gives that surety to the industry so that it knows we are sure-footed and can have that confidence. Without confidence, we are not going to get the investment into the country for the automotive industry or for other industries. That is why we are investing £7.5 billion to help businesses, drivers and manufacturers. That surety will help to bring that investment in.

passages.speaker: Lord Fox (LD)
passages.body: I thank the Minister for that Answer. This Question is about day-to-day operational costs. In March this year, the National Audit Office put those costs to the taxpayer at £1.3 million a day. What are the financial targets that we, the shareholders, are putting on British Steel? passages.title: Small and Medium-sized Enterprises
passages.speaker: The Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (Jonathan Reynolds)
passages.body: As official statistics show, despite considerable pressure arising from international events, British businesses continue to be resilient, and growth to the end of the year in September was back to over 2%. Small and medium-sized enterprises represent 99% of businesses in the UK, and they are the backbone of that resilience and success. The Department supports them in a number of ways, including increased access to finance, cutting regulation, increasing small business rates relief thresholds, and tackling late payments with the Commercial Payments Bill.

passages.title: Small and Medium-sized Enterprises
passages.speaker: Jonathan Reynolds
passages.body: come out of engagement with small business representative organisations and small businesses themselves. I direct Paul towards the business growth service, available at business.gov.uk, which provides a full list of interventions that might support him in his mission.

passages.title: Small Businesses: Bexleyheath and Crayford
passages.speaker: The Financial Secretary to the Treasury and Paymaster General (James Murray)
passages.body: As I was just saying, the Government are backing high streets and small businesses with a package that means that all retail, hospitality and leisure properties in England will see their business rates frozen in real terms, reduced or cut to zero. The Government are also helping employers, particularly small and medium employers, to recruit the workers that they need by expanding local apprenticeship services and providing eligible small and medium-sized enterprises with a £2,000 hiring payment when recruiting young workers.

passages.title: AI systems: NHS Data
passages.speaker: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (Baroness Lloyd of Effra) (Lab)
passages.body: My Lords, AI developers should keep their systems under safe control. We expect prompt, transparent reporting of unexpected behaviour. In respect of breach of systems, the Computer Misuse Act applies to AI developers, and they must not breach systems. If breaches happen, victims should be informed immediately. If personal data, such as NHS records, is accessed, the Information Commission should be informed within 72 hours. The cyber Bill strengthens protections for essential services such as NHS trusts. Regulated AI services must report significant loss of control incidents within 24 hours.

passages.title: AI systems: NHS Data

passages.body: The noble Lord is right to highlight the importance of data security and privacy as being fundamental to the operation of the NHS and those of its suppliers. There is guidance given to those in the NHS about that; there is also guidance from the Information Commission, as he will probably be more aware than I, about the standards that should be applied.

passages.speaker: Lord Roborough (Con)
passages.body: My Lords, the concerning levels of water in storage—17% beneath seasonal norms, as the Minister mentioned—reflects not just a dry year but systematic underinvestment by the water industry against long-standing forecasts for demand growth and climate change. What assessment have the Government made of the speed, cost and volume of improvement that is possible from nature-based solutions and on-farm reservoirs, versus the expense, controversy and long timelines of new reservoirs? I declare my interest as a farmer and landowner.

Genuine resilience and adaptation are needed.
